lesson.title: Building a Survey That Actually Works
lesson.summary: A trustworthy survey is a system of overlapping safeguards, probability sampling, full coverage, low nonresponse, and careful wording, each defending against a different way the results can go wrong.
lesson.body:
Designing a survey is not a single decision, it is a bundle of decisions, and each one defends against a specific way a survey can go wrong. A simple random sample defends against selection bias by giving every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen. A complete sampling frame defends against undercoverage by making sure no meaningful group of the target population is left out of the pool the sample is drawn from. Careful follow up procedures defend against nonresponse bias by keeping the group that fails to answer small and similar to the group that does answer. Careful wording and administration, covered in the previous two chapters, defend against response bias by keeping answers close to the truth. A survey is only as trustworthy as its weakest safeguard, since a flawless sample ruined by leading questions is just as useless as a well worded questionnaire sent to a badly biased sample.

Each safeguard targets a different point in the survey's life. Probability sampling happens at the moment of selection: instead of asking whoever is convenient, like shoppers walking past a table, a probability sample uses a formal random mechanism so every unit has a known chance of selection, which allows results to be generalized back to the population with a calculable margin of error. Coverage happens before selection begins, when the sampling frame is built; a phone survey using only landlines will systematically miss younger, cell only households no matter how randomly it dials within that flawed list. Nonresponse happens after selection, when some chosen people do not answer, and those people often differ from responders in ways that matter, such as being busier or harder to reach. Response bias happens at the moment of answering, driven by wording and format.

To see why all four safeguards matter together rather than separately, suppose, purely for illustration, that a survey's chance of avoiding a coverage problem is 0.90, its chance of avoiding a serious nonresponse problem is 0.80, and its chance of avoiding a response bias problem is 0.85, and suppose for simplicity that these three risks operate independently of one another. The multiplication rule for independent events says the probability of avoiding all three at once is the product of the individual probabilities: 0.90 times 0.80 times 0.85, which equals 0.612. By the complement rule, the probability that at least one problem slips through is 1 minus 0.612, or 0.388, meaning a survey built this way still has better than a one in three chance of carrying at least one meaningful flaw. Real safeguards are not perfectly independent, but the arithmetic illustrates why professional pollsters treat survey design as a system of overlapping defenses rather than trusting any single safeguard to catch everything.

In practice, large scale surveys combine several safeguards at once: an address based frame to reach cell and landline households, multiple contact attempts to push up response rates, questions pilot tested for neutral wording, and statistical adjustments afterward for whatever remains. No single fix is sufficient alone.

Notice how much of this chapter, and the two before it, has depended on probability without ever formally defining it: a known chance of selection, a probability of avoiding a flaw, a probability of a response. The next chapter finally builds that formal foundation, defining what probability actually means and how to work with it precisely, the exact toolkit needed to reason carefully about surveys, samples, and everything that follows.
